result: In double-decision tasks about color and motion, the accuracy of one decision is unaffected by the difficulty of the other decision. Sensitivity to variation in stimulus strength along each dimension is independent of the difficulty along the uninformative dimension, consistent with parallel, independent processing channels for color and motion.
evaluation: Claims C2, C18, C35-C37, C39, C216-C218 consistently demonstrate no interference in choice accuracy across multiple experiments and stimulus conditions. The logistic regression analysis (C37) and superposition of data points in Figure 2 provide statistical and visual support. This is consistent with established knowledge of parallel visual pathways (C40). Both serial and parallel models are consistent with this finding (C45).

result: Response times reveal that the two decisions do not form simultaneously; the double-decision time is the sum of the two single-decision times. The data are better explained by serial models than parallel models, as demonstrated by both drift-diffusion model fits and empirical RT distribution analyses.
evaluation: Claims C3, C19-C20, C42-C44 describe the RT pattern supporting seriality. Model comparison claims C46, C49, C56-C57, C224-C225, C227-C228 provide decisive statistical support (log10BF > 17 for empirical approach, log10BF > 66 for drift-diffusion approach) for serial over parallel models across 10 of 11 participants. The RT data show stacked bell-shaped curves (C43-C44) consistent with additive decision times.

result: Both stimulus dimensions are acquired in parallel for the initial ~0.1 s. In Experiment 2 with 120 ms stimulus duration, double-decisions were just as accurate as single-decision controls, and psychophysical reverse correlation showed identical influence of stimulus fluctuations on choices in single- and double-decision tasks.
evaluation: Claims C4, C67, C69-C70, C215, C233-C235, C237 converge on parallel acquisition. The lack of interference in choice accuracy at short durations (C67, C233-C234), identical psychophysical kernels (C70, C235), and reverse correlation analysis (Figure 3B) provide strong evidence. This was surprising given the serial RT pattern (C71) but is reconciled by the buffer model (C237).

result: After initial parallel acquisition, stimulus dimensions are incorporated serially in time-multiplexed bouts. Color and motion information are acquired in parallel but are unable to update the decision simultaneously, requiring serial incorporation into decision variables.
evaluation: Claims C5, C12, C23, C78, C80, C108, C160-C161, C180, C182-C183 describe the core finding of parallel acquisition followed by serial incorporation. This is supported by: (1) no interference in accuracy at short durations (Exp 2), (2) additive RTs (Exp 1), (3) interference at intermediate durations (Exp 3), and (4) competition before first termination (Exp 4). The model in Figure 8 provides a mechanistic explanation (C180, C182-C183).

result: There is a bottleneck that precludes updating more than one decision at a time, and buffers store samples of evidence while access to the decision is blocked. The bottleneck is located between the buffer and the update of the decision variable, specifically at the initiation of the dynamic process that implements updates in cortical circuits.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C13, C24-C25, C79, C82-C83, C166-C168, C170, C183-C184, C203, C240 describe the bottleneck and buffer architecture. The existence of buffers is inferred from parallel acquisition (Exp 2) combined with serial incorporation (Exp 1). The bottleneck location is inferred from the need for time to incorporate buffered information (C82) and the finite buffer duration (C83, C103). The bimanual task (Exp 4) demonstrates two buffers (C240). This confirms Pashler's response selection bottleneck (C24, C184).

result: Interference in accuracy occurs over a narrow range of stimulus viewing durations controlled by the experimenter. At intermediate durations (but not short durations), accuracy on one dimension suffers when the other dimension is difficult, explained by competition for processing time rather than sensory interference.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C85-C86, C91-C92, C97-C102, C107, C109-C112, C206, C219-C220 describe the prediction and confirmation of interference at intermediate durations in Experiment 3. The data show lower color sensitivity at intermediate durations when coupled with difficult motion (C98-C99), but not vice versa (C100), consistent with motion prioritization (C101-C102, C104). The interference is elusive (C110) because it requires three specific conditions to be satisfied. This is the only example of choice interference in the study (C109).

result: Model fits to Experiment 3 data suggest a buffer capacity of approximately 80 ms worth of stimulus information and prioritization of motion on approximately 80-96% of trials. Both purely serial and purely parallel buffer capacities provide very poor fits to the data.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 describe the buffer capacity estimate from Experiment 3. The best fits suggest ~80 ms buffer capacity (C103, Figure 4B) and 80-96% motion prioritization (C104). Model comparison shows that purely serial (buffer=0) and purely parallel (buffer=∞) models fit poorly (C106, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The serial and parallel models are special cases of the buffer model (C105).

result: The bimanual task confirms that the double-decision time is the sum of two sequential sampling processes, each with its own stopping time. The color and motion decisions compete before the first decision terminates, implying time-multiplexed alternation. Model comparison provides clear support for multiple switches with sparse alternations (average inter-switch interval ~704 ms).
evaluation: Claims C29-C31, C123-C127, C132-C142 describe findings from Experiment 4. The bimanual task provides direct evidence for two termination times (C29, C141) and competition before first termination (C30, C134-C135). The multi-switch model fits the data better than the single-switch model (C132-C136, Figure 6). Alternations were sparse with ~704 ms inter-switch intervals for 7 of 8 participants (C137-C138). This rules out target-wise integration models (C142).

result: A binary decision (same vs. different) based only on motion processing also exhibits additive decision times. The RTs for same-different judgments were almost twice as long as 1D direction judgments, suggesting serial incorporation. This demonstrates that serial incorporation is not restricted to different perceptual modalities and rules out Hick's law as an explanation.
evaluation: Claims C32, C149-C152, C155-C159 describe findings from Experiment 5. The same-different task shows additive decision times (C32, C152) with RTs almost twice as long as 1D judgments (C150). The pattern of RTs supports serial incorporation (C156) despite parallel acquisition (C155). This rules out Hick's law (C157) and demonstrates generality beyond color-motion (C158-C159). Model comparison favors serial over parallel (log10BF > 7 for both participants).

result: The bottleneck is responsible for the long timescales of many cognitive operations framed as decisions. It arises from an anatomical constraint: it is impossible to connect in parallel every possible source of evidence with neural circuits responsible for representing propositions or plans. The brain's routing problem holds the key to why many mental operations operate serially.
evaluation: Claims C8, C208, C241-C243 are speculative interpretations about the broader implications and neural basis of the bottleneck. While the existence of the bottleneck is well-supported by the experimental data, the claims about its responsibility for long timescales of cognitive operations (C8, C208) and its anatomical basis (C241-C242) are theoretical proposals rather than empirically tested hypotheses. The connection to the brain's routing problem (C243) is based on prior theoretical work (Zylberberg et al., 2010) but not directly tested here.

result: A conceptual framework is developed that accommodates findings from all five experiments with known neurobiology of 1D perceptual decisions. The model includes parallel acquisition through sensory filters, temporary storage in buffers, and serial incorporation into decision variables through a bottleneck. The bottleneck is between the buffer and the update of the decision variable, corresponding to the 'response selection' bottleneck hypothesized by Pashler.
evaluation: Claims C162-C206 describe the conceptual model in Figure 8. The model successfully reconciles: (1) parallel acquisition at short durations (C163-C164, C180-C182), (2) serial incorporation and additive RTs (C166-C167, C183-C184, C204-C205), (3) long RTs after brief stimuli (C181), and (4) interference at intermediate durations (C206). The model is compatible with neural data showing ~180 ms delays (C198) and is a variant of drift-diffusion models (C197). The diagrams are didactic (C199) and the logic generalizes beyond strict alternation (C201-C202).

result: Prior research has established that humans and monkeys accumulate noisy samples of evidence to a threshold in binary perceptual decisions, that there is a structural bottleneck in response selection, that color and motion are processed by parallel independent channels, and that performance continues to increase with stimulus duration up to at least 0.5 s in 1D tasks.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C15, C40, C64, C87, C210-C211 cite prior research that provides the foundation for the current study. These are well-established findings in the literature on perceptual decision-making (C9, C64, C87), the psychological refractory period (C10), and parallel visual processing (C40, C210-C211). The citations are appropriate and the claims accurately represent prior work.

result: The experimental tasks were designed to allow participants to integrate both streams of evidence simultaneously from the same location in the visual field and to indicate choices with eye or hand movements. Participants decided the dominant color and direction of motion in a small patch of dynamic random dots. The stimulus was designed to minimize interference or competition for spatial attention.
evaluation: Claims C11, C14, C17, C33, C63, C93-C96, C116-C122, C143-C148, C212-C213 describe the experimental design and methods. These are straightforward descriptions of the tasks, stimuli, and procedures used in the five experiments. The sample sizes, trial numbers, and stimulus parameters are clearly reported. The design choices (e.g., same location, same dots for color and motion) are appropriate for testing the hypotheses.

result: A prediction was made that with brief stimulus presentations, successful color decisions ought to be attained at the expense of motion, and vice versa (choice interference). This prediction was not confirmed in Experiment 2.
evaluation: Claims C21-C22, C62, C65-C66 describe a prediction based on the serial processing hypothesis and its disconfirmation in Experiment 2. The prediction was reasonable given the serial RT pattern (C21, C62, C65-C66), but the data showed no interference (C22, C67). This surprising result led to the revised model with buffers and parallel acquisition (C23, C69, C237).

result: The systematic underestimate of RT by both models on doubly difficult stimulus strengths arises because the drift-diffusion model assumes constant variance of momentary evidence across all stimulus strengths, but the variance is likely smaller near 0% coherence. This overestimate of variance leads to underestimate of RT in the middle of the graphs.
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 explain a systematic misfit of the drift-diffusion models. The explanation is based on known properties of neural responses to motion stimuli (C53, citing Britten et al., 1993; Shadlen et al., 2006). The restrictive assumption of constant variance (C52) is a known limitation of the drift-diffusion model. The inference about the consequence of this assumption (C54) is reasonable.

result: Limitations of Experiments 1-3 include lack of access to the completion time of each component decision and inability to discern the nature of serial processing (e.g., whether they alternate or one is prioritized). The strong support for serial processing does not specify where in the processing chain the seriality arises.
evaluation: Claims C61, C114-C115, C229 acknowledge limitations of the analyses in Experiments 1-3. These are appropriate caveats that motivated Experiment 4 (bimanual task) to address the limitations. The acknowledgment of limitations strengthens the overall argument by showing awareness of what can and cannot be concluded from each experiment.

result: In Experiment 2, the entire stimulus stream lasted only 120 ms, yet participants exhibited variation in response times as a function of stimulus strength. The fastest RTs were ~300 ms longer than the stimulus, and RTs were approximately 100-200 ms longer in double-decisions than in single decisions. Procrastination would not explain the difference between conditions.
evaluation: Claims C72-C77 describe RT patterns in Experiment 2. The long RTs despite brief stimuli (C72-C74) and the difference between single and double decisions (C75) are clearly shown in Figure 3A. The inference that procrastination cannot explain the difference (C76) is reasonable because procrastination would affect both conditions equally. The extra time is attributed to serial incorporation (C77-C78).

result: Speculations about the mechanism of serial processing in the double-decision RT task include that some kind of alternation must occur such that segments of one or the other stimulus stream is not incorporated into its decision. When the decision maker controls termination, they can compensate for missing information by collecting more until reaching the same terminating bound. When one process terminates, the rate of improvement of the other process should recover.
evaluation: Claims C81, C84, C90 are speculations and predictions based on the model. The speculation about alternation (C81) is later confirmed by the bimanual task (Exp 4). The explanation for why there is no interference in accuracy in the RT task (C84) is a reasonable inference from the model. The prediction about recovery after termination (C90) is tested in Experiment 3.

result: Two variants of the serial model are distinguished: the single-switch model (decision maker only switches when the first decision is completed) and the multi-switch model (decision maker can alternate between decisions before finalizing one). These models make different predictions for how the response time for the first decision depends on the difficulty of the second decision.
evaluation: Claims C113, C128-C131 describe the two variants of the serial model and their predictions. These are clear descriptions of the models and their distinguishing predictions. The single-switch model predicts independence of RT1st and D2nd difficulty (C130), while the multi-switch model predicts dependence (C131). These predictions are tested in Experiment 4 (Figure 6).

result: The present study extends the framework of bounded evidence accumulation to more complex decisions composed of the conjunction of two decisions about two distinct features. The experimental findings demonstrate that a double-decision about the dominant color and direction of motion is formed serially, which is surprising given parallel visual pathways. Evidence for seriality is adduced mainly from the pattern of double-decision RTs. The key to resolving the apparent contradiction with vision science is the short and variable duration experiments.
evaluation: Claims C207, C209, C221-C222, C226, C230-C233, C236, C238-C239 summarize the main contributions and logic of the study. The extension to complex decisions (C207) and the surprising finding of seriality (C209, C221) are well-supported. The emphasis on RT patterns as evidence for seriality (C222) is appropriate. The resolution of the apparent contradiction through Experiments 2 and 3 (C230-C233, C236) is a key insight. The acknowledgment of limitations (C226, C238) and the progression to Experiment 4 (C239) show the logical development of the argument.
